chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Overnight stays, departure times and musicians who missed Fletcher's bus
summary: Distance decided whether bands stayed overnight; Fletcher gave a half-hour grace before leaving, and some men hired a car after oversleeping.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Did you very often have to do directly from one job to the next, in other words, just finish the gig and get aboard the bus again and take off and drive the next 20 hours and --

Well, that would depend upon the distance of the next engagement. Like if you'd play a place tonight, like say Jacksonville, Florida, and you only had 200 miles to go. Well then, you'd stay all night in Jacksonville after you'd finished the date, which was a welcome sight, a welcome relief, we'll say, and you'd leave the next day around about, oh, 2:00 or 3:00 o'clock, if you didn't have to start playing until 9:00. The bus driver would usually check the conditions of the road that you were going to, you know, travel that next day, and if the map showed that the roads were very good, then you could make good time. We would leave at the latest time possible.

And I noticed a lot of times with Fletcher's band, if they were going to stay all night, Fletcher would say, we leave at 1:00 o'clock and the half hour -- we give you a half hour grace, meaning that you'd pull out at 1:30. And if there wasn't anybody there at that time, you would get there the best way you could. We lost a couple of guys a couple of times. They had to come in -- in fact, I remember a couple of musicians hired a private car to bring them in. They had missed the bus because they'd had such a ball.
The night before, you know, in that particular town -- and you just didn't wake up, man. And his
alibi was the alarm clock didn't go off. He didn't have an alarm clock.
His chick didn't wake him up.
That's the thing, yeah. And his company forgot, you know, sort of, and -- but he was all smiles. He didn't mind paying the dues. Those were great days.
